name: Push, periodic sync and background fetch
plain: Ways a site can wake its service worker after the person leaves: push messages, timed sync, long downloads.
meaning: Push needs a notification permission; Periodic Background Sync needs an installed PWA and site engagement, with a minimum of about 12 hours between wakes; Background Fetch shows a download notice. Each lets a site run code with no tab open.

access.persistence: Subscriptions last until the person unsubscribes, clears data, or the push service expires them
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

chrome.note: Push 50, periodic sync 80 for installed PWAs

ios_safari.note: Push only for Home Screen web apps

limits.headline: Can wake a site's background script after you leave, through push, timed sync or downloads
limits.user_action: You allow notifications, install a web app, or start a big download
can: Wake the site through a push message once you allow notifications
Refresh an installed web app about once every 12 hours or more
Run a large download that shows a progress notice
Run site code with no tab open for a short time
cannot: Use push without your notification permission
Use timed sync unless the site is installed and you use it often
Run in the background without limits, since browsers stop it after a short time
Work the same in Safari and Firefox, which support less
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge support all three. Firefox and Safari, including iPhone browsers, support only some.

story.what_it_is: Several ways a site can wake its background script after you leave: push messages, timed syncs, long downloads.

marketing.name: Push API
marketing.pitch: Lets a server send messages that wake the web app, even when it is closed.

story.for_you: After you leave the page, the site may still run small bits of code when it gets a push, a timed sync or a download event. You mostly see a notification or fresher content on return.
story.for_makers: Makers use these to stay in touch, keep apps fresh and finish work after the tab closes. They are also a way for a site to run code you did not open. Browsers limit it by permission and by how often you use the site.

use_cases.example: A web chat wakes on push and shows a new message, so you do not have to open the page.
A news app wakes on a timer to load the latest stories before you open it.
A streaming web app finishes a movie download after you close the tab.
A browser game wakes on push to tell you a match is ready.
An ad network wakes a site's background script to show a promo notice.
A site wakes in the background to send queued usage data it could not send before.
A bank wakes on push to show a login approval prompt.

technical_bounds: Periodic sync minimum about 12 hours and only for installed PWAs (Chrome)
Silent push is not allowed: Chrome and Safari require a user visible notification
Safari push only for Home Screen web apps on iOS

history.change: Periodic Background Sync for installed PWAs
Web Push for Home Screen web apps and macOS Safari
